title: 14 Content marketing tips to improve your brand visibility
summary: Use these 14 content marketing tips to plan, create, distribute, and optimize content that‘s built to be found and cited in search and AI answers
body_markdown:
Content marketing tips that improve brand visibility can be loosely organized into four objectives: aligning content with a real audience need and business goal, maximizing the value of finding and citing content, planning content distribution from the start, and measuring content outcomes over pageviews.


Failing to achieve any one of these used to cost you traffic. Now it can also cost you a place in an AI answer. When someone asks ChatGPT or Google AI Mode about your niche, the response often names just a few brands, with the rest never getting any visibility.


These 14 tips for content marketing cover all four objectives in order, with step-by-step workflows for research and optimization.


## Plan before you create


Planning content before creating it means deciding who each piece is for, what its job is, and which questions it answers. Knowing all this ahead of time allows you to judge how successful the content was later.


If you don't yet have a content marketing strategy, start with our guides on[content marketing strategy](https://www.semrush.com/blog/content-marketing-strategy-guide/) and[content marketing best practices](https://www.semrush.com/blog/content-marketing-best-practices/) .


The tips below will help each piece of content you create succeed according to your strategy.


### 1. Build audience personas from real research


Build audience personas according to what real customers say and do, because personas based on assumptions can lead you toward topics your audience isn't looking for.


An audience persona is a semi-fictional profile of one customer segment: who they are, what they're trying to achieve, what gets in their way, and the questions they ask before buying. Strong personas draw on data like:


- Questions that repeatedly come up in sales and support conversations
- Reviews of both your products and your competitors' products
- Customer interviews and surveys
- Discussions in communities where your audience is found, such as Reddit or niche forums


To add audience data, enter your domain and up to four competitors in Semrush's[Traffic & Market Toolkit](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/traffic/) , then click " **Analyze** ." For example, Counter Culture Coffee could compare counterculturecoffee.com with bluebottlecoffee.com and stumptowncoffee.com.


Then open the[Demographics](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/traffic/demographics) report to see each audience’s age, location, and sex so you can describe who each persona represents.


Next, open the[Socioeconomics](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/traffic/socioeconomics) report to compare household size, income, employment, and education, which helps you determine what each persona can afford.


Finally, open the[Behavior](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/traffic/behavior/) report to discover which social platforms each audience uses so that you’ll know where you can reach them. For example, Counter Culture’s audience is more active on Reddit and Instagram than Blue Bottle’s or Stumptown’s, which makes Reddit’s coffee communities a good place to look for the questions their customers ask.


Combine the tool data with what you learn from customers into one profile per segment, and note the platforms each segment uses. You’ll use those platforms in tip nine.


### 2. Map your content to the buyer's journey


Map every piece of content to both an audience and a stage of the[buyer’s journey](https://www.semrush.com/blog/buyers-journey/) , then give it one measurable job. This level of planning gives you the precise knowledge of what to create for each stage and how to judge each piece.


The[content marketing funnel](https://www.semrush.com/blog/content-marketing-funnel/) splits that journey into three stages, and content has a different job in each stage:


1. **Top of funnel (TOFU):** People are learning about a problem or interest, so content’s job is awareness. How-to guides and explainers fit here, like a roaster's guide to brewing pour-over coffee at home.
2. **Middle of funnel (MOFU):** People are comparing options, so content’s job is supporting their evaluation. Comparison pages and buying guides fit here, like a guide to choosing between light and dark roasts.
3. **Bottom of funnel (BOFU):** People are ready to choose, so content’s job is capturing leads or driving conversions. Case studies, customer stories, and offer pages fit here, like a subscription page that features customer reviews.


Write the job into the content brief for each piece, such as "earn newsletter signups" or "support comparison research." That gives every piece one measure of success to track in tip 13 later.


To spot stages your content hasn’t covered, tag your existing content by stage. If most of your library sits at the top of the funnel, buyers who are ready to compare or choose won't find your brand when it matters most.


### 3. Prioritize search intent over keyword volume


Prioritize keywords and prompts by their intent rather than search volume alone. A specific, low-volume query often comes from someone much closer to making a decision than a broad, high-volume one.


Take two keywords a specialty roaster might target. According to Semrush’s[Keyword Overview](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/keywordoverview/) , “coffee beans” gets approximately 60,500 monthly searches in the U.S., and “best coffee beans for pour over” gets about 320.


Semrush labels both keywords with commercial[search intent](https://www.semrush.com/blog/search-intent/) , but they come from different buyers. Someone searching “best coffee beans for pour over” already brews pour-over at home and is choosing what to buy next, which makes them a close match for a roaster’s product pages. The term is also easier to rank for, with a keyword difficulty (KD) score of 14 vs. 23 for “coffee beans.”


The same approach applies to AI prompts. Someone asking ChatGPT which beans suit a pour-over setup and produce fruity flavors is further along the funnel than someone asking how coffee beans are roasted.


Keywords and prompts like these belong to one topic — a group of related keywords and AI prompts about one subject. When you plan content for a topic, prioritize its specific questions and not just its biggest keyword. Your[SEO and content marketing](https://www.semrush.com/blog/seo-and-content-marketing/) efforts will then match what different searchers need in different stages of the funnel for that topic.


Next, tip four will show you how to find terms like these with[Keyword Gap](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/keywordgap/) .


### 4. Find and fill content gaps


Find the topics where competitors appear in search results and AI answers but you don’t. Then create or update content to cover these gaps so your rivals aren’t the default answer in your market.


A content gap is a topic your audience cares about that competitors cover and you don’t. Gaps show where your topic visibility (how often your brand appears in Google results and AI answers for a topic compared with competitors) falls behind your rivals. Start with search gaps.


Open[Keyword Gap](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/keywordgap/) , enter your domain and up to four competitor domains, and click “ **Compare** .”


In the results table, review two tabs:


- “ **Missing** ”: Keywords every competitor you entered ranks for but you don’t
- “ **Untapped** ”: Keywords at least one competitor ranks for but you don’t


Not every gap is worth closing. Counter Culture’s “Missing” tab includes brewing terms like “french press” and “chemex,” which fit a roaster’s how-to guides, alongside terms like “lift top coffee table” and other coffee brands’ names, which are less relevant.


AI answers to prompts can also mention competitors and completely omit your brand. To find these gaps, use the[Visibility Overview](https://www.semrush.com/ai-seo/overview/) in Semrush’s AI Visibility Toolkit:


1. Enter your domain and click “ **Analyze** ”
2. In the “Topics & Sources” section, add your competitors above the table and click “ **Analyze** ” again
3. Open the “ **Topic Opportunities** ” tab and sort by “ **Competitors Mentioned** ”


Counter Culture’s report lists more than 3,500 topics where Blue Bottle or Stumptown appear in AI answers and Counter Culture doesn’t. Switch the view to “ **Prompts** ” to see the full individual prompt.


Filter both lists against the personas from tip one, and drop anything your audience wouldn’t care about. For each topic remaining, check whether an existing page could cover it first (see tip 12 ).


Finally, click “ **Monitor all prompts** ” next to the topics you decide to cover so you can track whether your brand starts appearing for them.


## Create content worth ranking and citing


Creating content worth ranking and citing means giving readers unique content they can't get elsewhere and making your answers easy to find, understand, and quote — for search engines and AI systems alike.


### 5. Publish original research and primary data


Publish original research and primary data because it gives publishers and AI systems an original source to reference, which can earn your brand mentions, citations, and leads.


Original research can take several forms:


- Survey-based reports
- Analyses of your own product, customer, or sales data
- Industry benchmark reports


Exit Five, a community for B2B marketers,[published a salary report](https://www.exitfive.com/newsletter/how-much-should-you-be-getting-paid-as-a-b2b-marketer/) in 2025 built on responses from 1,079 full-time, in-house B2B marketers. It offered the report as a[lead magnet](https://www.semrush.com/blog/what-is-lead-magnet/) : readers were required to enter their email address to get it.


[Bani Kaur](https://www.linkedin.com/in/bani-kaur-/) , Freelance Content Strategist, helped create the report, which had received just over 8,000 downloads as of September 2025. She recommends checking the internal data you already have before commissioning new research:


> *“Say you’re a project management tool with 10K users. A few simple cross sections could reveal how teams of different sizes structure projects, how long tasks stay open, or how completion rates shift across industries. That’s gold for your audience — and it costs you nothing beyond the analysis and a good storyteller to pull it together.”*


The same approach applies beyond software. For example, a specialty coffee roaster could publish what its subscription data shows about which roast levels customers reorder most often. Findings like these are hard to replicate, which is a big part of what makes[quality content](https://www.semrush.com/blog/quality-content/) worth citing.


### 6. Structure content to be AI-citable


Use an AI-citable content structure by opening each section with a clear takeaway that makes sense independent of additional context. Clear summaries and question-and-answer formatting are both associated with AI citations.


Our[study of AI citations](https://www.semrush.com/blog/content-optimization-ai-search-study/) compared 304,805 URLs cited by ChatGPT Search, Google AI Mode, and Perplexity with URLs ranking in Google's top 20 for related keywords (July-August 2025). Cited pages scored 32.83% higher for clarity and summarization and 25.45% higher for question-and-answer formatting.


These findings show association rather than causation, but they point to four structural techniques:


- **Headings that answer or ask:** Write each heading so it states the section's takeaway or asks the question your reader would ask
- **Answer-first sections:** Open each section with a one- or two-sentence answer so readers can immediately see that it addresses what the heading asks
- **Q&A blocks:** Use question-and-answer formatting, like FAQ sections, where readers expect direct, concise answers
- **Named entities and defined terms:** Define each specialist term the first time you use it, and name products, brands, and concepts instead of relying on "it" or "this"


For example, a roaster's brewing guide might change a heading from "Grind size" to "What grind size works best for pour-over?" and open the section with a direct answer:


*Use a medium-fine grind, about the texture of table salt, because it lets water evenly pass through the grounds for a balanced cup.*


### 7. Experiment with formats deliberately


Experiment with formats deliberately by testing one new format at a time and compare it with your existing formats according to the same metrics. The results will indicate which formats deserve more of your production time.


Formats worth testing include:


- Expert interviews
- Case studies
- Short- and long-form videos
- Webinars
- Podcast episodes
- [User-generated content](https://www.semrush.com/blog/user-generated-content/)
- Ebooks and whitepapers
- [Infographics](https://www.semrush.com/blog/what-is-an-infographic/)
- Templates and calculators


For example, a coffee roaster who already has a written guide on brewing pour-over coffee could publish a short video on the same topic. Keeping the topic the same makes it easier to see what changing the format itself causes.


To keep the comparison fair, judge both formats over the same window, such as one quarter, and compare engagement, traffic to your site, and AI mentions. Rankings won’t compare well here, as the guide format will compete in Google’s search results while the video will mostly appear on YouTube.


### 8. Prioritize UX and readability


Prioritize user experience (UX) and readability by making content easy to scan, read, and use on any device. Readers who find what they need quickly stay longer and are more likely to come back.


To improve UX and readability:


- Add captions or subtitles to videos so people can watch without sound
- Add[alt text](https://www.semrush.com/blog/alt-text/) to images for screen readers and search engines
- Check that text, including text inside images, is legible on small screens
- Use descriptive[anchor text](https://www.semrush.com/blog/anchor-text/) so readers know what a link leads to
- Use clear subheadings so readers can scan the page
- Limit paragraph length to a few sentences


Several of these, like clear subheadings and short paragraphs, also make sections easier for AI systems to understand and extract, which builds on the structure from tip six.


To check readability, paste your draft into[Hemingway Editor](https://hemingwayapp.com/help/docs/readability) , which scores text by U.S. grade level. Its paid Plus version targets grade nine by default, which Hemingway describes as the average reading level for U.S. adults. Aim for that level or below, and edit the sentences the tool highlights. If you’re refreshing an existing page, Semrush’s Content Optimizer also checks readability (see tip 12 ).


## Distribute as deliberately as you create


Distributing content as deliberately as you create it means treating promotion as part of the content plan and not as an afterthought. Even strong content won’t earn results if the right people never see it.


### 9. Plan content distribution before production


Plan content distribution before production by setting each piece's channels, formats, owner, and promotion timeline up front. Assets will be built for where they’ll run instead of getting adapted afterward.


A distribution plan covers five decisions:


1. **Audience:** The persona and journey stage the piece serves, from tips one and two
2. **Channels:** Where that audience already spends time, such as the platforms in the Behavior report from tip one
3. **Formats:** Which version of the piece each channel receives (tip 10 covers how to adapt them)
4. **Owner:** The person responsible for publishing and promoting the piece on each channel
5. **Timeline:** When each format releases, such as the carousel on publish day and the newsletter mention two days later


For example, Counter Culture’s audience data from tip one indicated Instagram and Reddit. So, a plan for a new pour-over brewing guide might include a carousel of the brewing steps for Instagram and answers to pour-over questions in Reddit’s coffee communities, with a link to the guide where relevant.


Planning early changes what you create. Bani, who helped build the Exit Five salary report from tip five, built distribution into the report’s graphics:


> *"When we designed the Exit Five B2B Salary report, I worked with my design team to build in distribution. For every graph we made, we thought, 'How does this lend itself to the newsletter?' or, 'Let's present this info such that people can't help but share!' or, 'Let's make this perfectly screenshot-able.'"*


Add each plan to your[content calendar](https://www.semrush.com/blog/content-calendar/) , so promotion dates sit next to publish dates.


### 10. Repurpose one idea across channels


Repurpose one idea across channels by turning a single strong piece of content into several channel-specific formats. You’ll reach more of your audience without needing to invent new topics every week.


One pillar piece can feed every channel in your distribution plan. Counter Culture's pour-over guide, for example, could transform into a YouTube demonstration, Instagram carousel of the steps, newsletter tip, and LinkedIn post about how its baristas test brew recipes.


Adapt each version to how people use that channel rather than simply copying the same text everywhere.


[Stella Inabo](https://www.linkedin.com/in/stella-inabo-/) , Editor in Chief for The Geek Circle, considers platform behavior when choosing formats:


> *"If someone is scrolling through LinkedIn and sees a video, they're likely to expect a sound bite that's interesting, controversial, or thought-provoking."*


[Repurposing tools](https://www.semrush.com/blog/content-repurposing-tools/) like these speed up the creation of each version:


- [Semrush’s AI Video Marketing Automator](https://www.semrush.com/apps/ai-video-marketing-automator/) turns blog posts into videos for YouTube, TikTok, and Instagram
- [Semrush’s AI Social Content Generator](https://www.semrush.com/apps/ai-social-content-generator/) repurposes blog content into social media posts
- [2short.ai](https://2short.ai/) finds the most engaging moments in a long video and cuts them into short clips
- [Gemini Notebook](https://notebooklm.google.com/) (formerly NotebookLM) turns existing content into explainer videos


### 11. Promote content across owned and paid channels


Promote your content across both owned and paid channels by sharing every piece through the audiences you've already built, then add paid promotion when the piece has a commercial or lead-generation job worth the expense.


Start with owned channels like your email list, social profiles, and links from related pages on your site. These have no additional costs and reach people who already know you.


For pieces that require additional reach, consider these paid options:


- **Influencer partnerships:** Pay creators your audience follows to share the piece with their followers
- **Social ads:** Boost posts that already perform well organically, using a platform like[Meta Ads Manager](https://www.facebook.com/business/tools/ads-manager) , so you start with proven creative (see our guide to[paid social](https://www.semrush.com/blog/paid-social/) )
- **Newsletter ads:** Use a marketplace like[Paved](https://www.paved.com/) , which connects advertisers with newsletters that sell sponsorships, so you can sponsor newsletters your audience reads
- **Display ads:** Place promotions on websites and apps your audience visits, using[Google Ads](https://business.google.com/us/google-ads/) or another ad platform
- **Search ads:** Bid on keywords related to the piece so it appears at the top of[paid search results](https://www.semrush.com/blog/paid-search-ads/)


The pieces that justify paid spend are BOFU pages, original research, webinars, and gated assets, because they can turn paid reach into leads or sales. A TOFU explainer usually can't.


## Optimize and maintain what works


Optimizing and maintaining content that works requires measuring each piece against its job and deciding what to update, expand, or build around it, as published content tends to lose visibility over time without regular upkeep.


This is also where you discover which of the content marketing tips you’ve utilized have actually improved your numbers.


### 12. Know when to update vs. create new content


To determine whether you should update or create new content, check if an existing page already serves the searcher’s need: update the content if one does, and create a new page only if you have a content gap. Otherwise, you risk creating two pages that compete for the same searches.


Use this rule of thumb:


- **Update content** when a page already ranks or earns impressions for the topic and the gap is freshness or completeness, like outdated product names, old screenshots, or a missing subtopic
- **Create new content** when no existing page matches the intent, or when covering the topic would pull an existing page away from its main job


For example, if Counter Culture's pour-over brewing guide ranks but skips grind size, the fix is an update. However, "best coffee beans for pour over" from tip three needs a different page entirely, because a how-to guide doesn't serve someone choosing what to buy.


Pages that still get traffic are often the most urgent to update.[Heike Young](https://www.linkedin.com/in/heikeyoung/) , former Head of Content, Social, and Integrated Marketing at Microsoft, says one of the first things she did at a previous company was audit its content:


> *"I quickly spotted some very old pieces of content that were still driving lots of traffic. They had outdated messaging, product names, and next steps. We prioritized fixing those to create a much better audience journey."*


Heike recommends repeating audits and refreshes at least once per year.


To find those pages, open the " **Pages and screens** " report in[Google Analytics 4 (GA4)](https://analytics.google.com/) , which ranks pages by views, and check the top results for outdated products, pricing, or next steps.


Next, find pages with declining rankings in[Google Search Console](https://search.google.com/search-console/) (GSC):


1. Click " **Performance** ," then check " **Average position** " and uncheck " **Total clicks** " and " **Total impressions** " so the chart shows rankings only
2. Click " **More** " to open the date range options, open the " **Compare** " tab, choose the two periods, and click " **Apply** "
3. Scroll down, open the “ **Pages** ” tab, and sort by the difference column to see which pages lost the most ground (a higher position number means a lower ranking)


Once you've decided a page is worth updating, open Semrush's[Content Optimizer](https://www.semrush.com/content/board/optimize) , enter the page's URL or paste its text, and click " **Optimize article** ."


In the editor, add your " **Audience location** " and “ **Keywords** ,” then click " **Submit** ."


Next click " **Edit target** " and change the "Readability level" from the default "College" to " **High school** ," which suits most general audiences.


Start with the "AI SEO" suggestions because they match the structure moves in tip six, and skip any suggestion that would make the page harder to read. For more on deciding what to refresh, see our guides on[when to update blog content](https://www.semrush.com/blog/when-to-update-blog-content/) and[content optimization](https://www.semrush.com/blog/content-optimization/) .


### 13. Connect content metrics to business outcomes


Connect content metrics to business outcomes by measuring each piece against the job you gave it in tip two. Treat rankings, traffic, engagement, shares, and AI visibility as leading signals, and treat downloads, signups, leads, and sales as the outcomes that show whether the content is producing results.


Here's how signals and outcomes line up for each job:


- **Awareness:** Track impressions, rankings, and AI mentions, and look for growth in returning visitors and branded searches
- **Evaluation support:** Track engagement and AI mentions for comparison prompts, and look for assisted conversions from people who read the page before buying
- **Lead capture:** Track traffic and clicks to the form, and look for downloads, signups, and qualified leads
- **Conversion:** Track traffic to the page, and look for sales, subscriptions, or influenced pipeline


For AI visibility, the[Visibility Overview](https://www.semrush.com/ai-seo/overview/) from tip four shows how often AI answers mention your brand ("Mentions"), how often they link to your content ("Citations"), and which pages get cited ("Cited Pages"). People rarely click through from AI answers, so mentions and citations will usually move before traffic does.


Review leading signals monthly and outcomes quarterly, since outcomes like leads and sales take longer to show a pattern. Our guide to[content marketing metrics](https://www.semrush.com/blog/content-marketing-metrics/) covers each metric in more detail.


### 14. Build topic clusters for authority


Build[topic clusters](https://www.semrush.com/blog/topic-clusters/) for authority by publishing a pillar page on a broad topic and linking it to pages on related subtopics. This practice makes it clear to search engines and AI systems that your site covers that topic in depth.


Clusters help build topical authority: how strongly search engines and AI systems associate your brand with a topic. But topical authority also depends on mentions elsewhere, like reviews, press coverage, communities, and other publishers. The original research and promotion in tips five, nine, 10, and 11 helps you earn those mentions.


To plan a topic cluster, open Semrush’s[Keyword Strategy Builder](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/keywordmanager/) :


1. Enter up to five seed keywords, like “pour over coffee,” and click “ **Create** ”
2. Open the “ **Topics and pages** ” tab and select the “ **Best for Strategy** ” filter, which balances keyword difficulty, search volume, and relevance. Each topic shows a pillar page and its subpages, so you get a ready-made cluster.
3. Click “ **Generate content** ” next to a page, then choose either “ **Article** ” to draft it in Content Optimizer or “ **SEO brief** ” to plan it first


\[Image request\]


As you publish each page, link it to the pillar and to related pages in the cluster with[internal links](https://www.semrush.com/blog/internal-links/) .


## Content marketing tips checklist


This checklist condenses the content marketing advice above into one line per tip, in workflow order, so you can check each piece before and after it goes live:


1. Base personas on customer research and audience data
2. Give every piece an audience, a journey stage, and one measurable job
3. Choose keywords and prompts by the need behind them, not volume alone
4. Check for keyword gaps and topic opportunities for missing content your audience cares about
5. Publish original research when you have data others don't
6. Open each section with a direct answer under a clear heading
7. Test one new format at a time against an existing one
8. Check readability against a grade nine target and legibility on small screens
9. Set channels, formats, owner, and timeline before production starts
10. Turn each strong piece into versions for every planned channel
11. Promote through owned channels first; pay only for commercial-intent or lead-gen pieces
12. Update pages that already serve an intent before creating new ones
13. Measure each piece against its job, with AI mentions as a leading signal
14. Link each new page into a topic cluster

## Put these content marketing tips to use


The content that routinely appears in search results and AI answers tends to have a clear job, reason to be cited, plan to reach its audience, and clear measure of whether it’s working. The best content marketing tips compound when they work together, but you don’t need all 14 at once. Start with the stage where your results lag most. Pick one content marketing tip from that stage, apply it to a page you already have, and measure it against its job.


To see how often AI answers mention your brand and where competitors appear instead, try Semrush's AI Visibility Toolkit.
